name: Makary Kotoko
confidence_why: Allison's grammar of Makary Kotoko (2012, 2020) and Mahamat's 2005 phonology both describe a pure tone language and say nothing of word stress, and Tourneux's 2021 review, which floats the idea that Allison's mid tone might be a weak accent on low-toned syllables, offers it only as a tentative explanation of the mid tone and does not claim stress in the ordinary sense.

new_statements.translation: Following an 'anonymous reviewer' cited by SA [Sean Allison] (p. 25, note 13), we will venture to sketch a possible solution to explain the mid[-tone] realisations. In the table below, B [= bas] denotes an accented syllable with low tone; H, an accented syllable with high tone. [...] This accent would today have a very weak distinctive value. If we rely on SA (pp. 25 and 483), here are the examples noted (in the ACCENTED column, our notation): UNACCENTED wò 'village' / ACCENTED 'wò (SA wō) 'summit'; gà 'mouth' / 'gà (SA gā) 'portion'; mɓì 'oil' / m̀'ɓì (SA mɓī) 'flour'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Makary Kotoko is a tone language (Allison: L, M, H, F, R on syllables; lexical and grammatical tone; Tourneux and Adam: two registers H/L). No published description locates word stress. The only stress statement is Tourneux's tentative reanalysis in his review of Allison 2020: the surface mid tone that Allison treats as a third phonemic level is reinterpreted as an 'accent' (stress) on a low- or high-toned syllable, lexically placed (it distinguishes a handful of near-minimal pairs, e.g. wò 'village' vs 'wò 'summit'), and 'of very weak distinctive value today'. If accepted, the accent is lexically specified, not positionally fixed; it can fall on the first or a non-first syllable (his table has BHB → BHM, BBB → MMB etc.).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the proposal is explicitly hedged ('nous nous risquerons à ébaucher une piste de solution') and rests on three near-minimal pairs taken from Allison 2020 pp. 25 and 483.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated lexemes and citation forms cited from Allison's phonology chapter and lexicon). Allison 2012, the accessible primary description, has a full tone section (pp. 26-37, F0 measurements p. 29) and says nothing at all about stress or accent; his 2020 'word' chapter lists pause, isolatability, meaning and tone assignment — not stress — as phonological-word criteria.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Makary Kotoko = the Mpade of Makary (Makari) town, Cameroon, i.e. the language-level mpad1242 (Glottolog also lists a Ngala/Ngal dialect ngal1301 not covered). Tourneux's accent remark draws an explicit parallel with the neighbouring Afade variety (afad1236), where he observed the same mid-level realisations; Allison's data come from Makary speakers (consultant Kaigama Malamine).

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees on stress because none of the primary descriptions mentions it: Allison 2006 (orthography statement, four surface tones), Mahamat 2005 (DEA thesis, two underlying register tones), and Allison 2012 (dissertation already held by the project, tone ch. 2.5, no stress statement) all describe Makary Kotoko purely as a tone language. The only stress-related statement remains Tourneux's 2021 review, which is a hedged reviewer's reanalysis of Allison's mid tone as a possible weak 'accent' rather than a first-hand description; the two works opened here neither confirm nor refute it. Secondary Google Books snippets (Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody, citing Allison 2012: 38: '.. no stress, rather only tone') point the same way but the governing clause was never visible. The catalog record's empty rule is therefore right to stay empty; the best-supported reading is 'tonal, no stress statement in the primary sources' with Tourneux's proposal noted as tentative.

sources.note: Describes the language as a two-tone register system and says nothing about stress; neither supports nor contradicts Tourneux 2021's tentative accent reanalysis. Note the tone inventory differs from Allison's (2 underlying tones H/L vs Allison's four surface tones incl. M and falling), but that is about tone, not stress.
